source: Lung cancer is expected to account for more than 1.80 million deaths worldwide in 2021, making it the top cause of cancer-related mortality (Siegel et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Siegel et al., 2021, which provides the statistical data about lung cancer mortality.

claim: In early stage (stages I and II) non-small cell lung carcinomas (NSCLC), surgical resection remains the therapy of choice.
source: In early stage (stages I and II) non-small cell lung carcinomas (NSCLC), surgical resection remains the therapy of choice.
evidence: This claim reflects established medical knowledge about the standard treatment for early stage NSCLC.

claim: Almost 40–55% of early stage NSCLC tumours recur following surgery.
source: However, almost 40–55% of these tumours recur following surgery (Ambrogi et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ambrogi et al., 2011, which provides the recurrence rate data.

claim: The TNM staging system of lung cancer based on the anatomic extent of disease is well recognised and widely adopted.
source: Currently, TNM staging system of lung cancer based on the anatomic extent of disease is well recognised and widely adopted, which allows tumours of comparable anatomic extent to be grouped together (Goldstraw et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Goldstraw et al., 2016, and reflects established medical knowledge about TNM staging.

claim: Individual characteristics, histology, and/or therapy characteristics may impact survival results, as seen by variation within stage groups.
source: Staging guides treatment and provides a broad prediction of prognosis, however individual characteristics, histology, and/or therapy characteristics may impact survival results, as seen by variation within stage groups.
evidence: This claim is based on established medical knowledge about the limitations of TNM staging and factors affecting prognosis.

claim: Non-anatomical predictors such as gene mutations and biomarker profiles were proposed to be incorporated in the refinement of the staging system.
source: In the refinement of the staging system, non-anatomical predictors such as gene mutations and biomarker profiles were proposed to be incorporated (Giroux et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Giroux et al., 2018, which discusses proposals for staging system refinement.

claim: The gene profiling approach relies on tissue sampling and may not fully explain the intratumoural heterogeneity seen in NSCLC.
source: However, the gene profiling approach relies on tissue sampling, and in addition, may not fully explain the intratumoural heterogeneity seen in NSCLC.
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge about the limitations of gene profiling approaches.

claim: Gene profiling tests have barriers in deploying to routine oncology workflows due to high turnaround time, complexity, and cost.
source: Besides, such tests have barriers in deploying to routine oncology workflows due to high turnaround time, complexity, and cost (Malone et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Malone et al., 2020, which discusses barriers to implementing gene profiling tests.

claim: Prognostic predictors such as TNM system and radiomics have been widely used to describe tumours.
source: To predict the patient's prognosis and to optimise individual clinical management, prognostic predictors such as TNM system and imaging-based high throughput quantitative biomarkers, radiomics, have been widely used to describe tumours (Du et al., 2019; Aonpong et al., 2020; Bera et al., 2022; Carmody et al., 1980; Chirra et al., 2019; Mirsadraee et al., 2012; van Griethuysen et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations documenting the use of TNM and radiomics in prognosis prediction.

claim: Deep learning models have recently been regarded as potentially valuable tools in cancer prognosis.
source: Artificial intelligence (AI) methods, especially some deep learning (DL) models, have recently been regarded as potentially valuable tools (Chilamkurthy et al., 2018; Nabulsi et al., 2021; Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating the value of deep learning in medical applications.

claim: DL models generated multiple quantitative assessments for tumour characteristics, which have the potential to describe tumour phenotypes with more predictive power than the clinical model.
source: DL models generated multiple quantitative assessments for tumour characteristics, which have the potential to describe tumour phenotypes with more predictive power than the clinical model (Xu et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Xu et al., 2019, which discusses the predictive power of DL models.

claim: Most AI-based methods do not take interdependencies and relationships between anatomical structures into account, leading to instability and poor generalisation of performance.
source: While the anatomical structures in a medical image are functionally and mechanically related, most AI-based methods do not take these interdependencies and relationships into account. This leads to instability and poor generalisation of performance (Zhou et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhou et al., 2021, which discusses limitations of AI-based methods.

claim: The Transformer model permits exceptional capabilities in natural language processing fields such as language translation.
source: Notably, the Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) model permits exceptional capabilities in natural language processing fields such as language translation and was later applied to the computer vision field and outperformed all state-of-the-art models given large amounts of training data (Dosovitskiy et al., 2020).

claim: The Transformer model was later applied to the computer vision field and outperformed all state-of-the-art models given large amounts of training data.
